title: HSBC Dialed Back Its Big Global Stock Call - Finimize
text: Bookmarks Free Newsletter Free Newsletter Ideas Guides Events For Business Bookmarks Browse News News Research Research Markets Markets HSBC Dialed Back Its Big Global Stock Call The bank downgraded global equities to neutral and upgraded sovereign bonds, pointing to Middle East tensions and AI regulation worries around the US midterm elections. Finimize Newsroom 1 min What's going on here? HSBC, one of Europe’s biggest banks, just stepped back from its most bullish view on global stocks, cutting equities to “neutral” and upgrading developed-market government bonds as Middle East tensions and US election-year tech policy worries pile up. What does this mean? Until recently, HSBC had its house view set to “max overweight” equities and “max underweight” developed-market sovereign bonds – basically, a strong preference for stocks over government debt. In a Monday note, it said the news cycle has become messy enough that it no longer wants to hold such an extreme stance. The bank double-upgraded those government bonds to “overweight,” arguing they could h.. ould hold up if tighter AI rules slow parts of the economy, or if post-election gridlock reduces the risk of big new spending plans. At the same time, HSBC flagged that markets may be too confident about one party winning decisively, and it also tweaked other calls, including being more cautious on the eurozone and emerging-market stocks. Why should I care? For markets: HSBC’s flip from max underweight to overweight boosts the case for government bonds. A move this big is more than a change of mood: large banks’ “house views” often feed into how institutions set asset -allocation targets. If some clients rebalance even slightly toward developed-market government bonds (think US Treasuries, German bunds, and UK gilts), that incremental demand can push prices up and yields down – yields move opposite prices. And because these bonds tend to do best when investors get nervous about growth, the shift could give sovereign debt a relative edge over global equities during a stretch when geopolitics and election-related regulation headlines are likely to keep volatility elevated.
